idiom_name: Iterator adapter chain (map/filter/flat_map/scan) consumed by a terminal
implementation_notes: Rust's Iterator trait is the pattern's shape: any transformation is a function from an Iterator to another Iterator (the adapters map/filter/flat_map/filter_map/scan), so a pipeline is ordinary method chaining, the source only has to be IntoIterator (range, slice, file lines, channel receiver, custom impl) and the destination is chosen by the terminal (collect into any FromIterator, fold, sum, for_each, find). What replaces the classic structure: iterator adapters plus closures replace a reducing-function transformer, with the compiler inlining the whole chain into one loop and no intermediate collection; scan gives stateful stages, and collect into Result or try_fold supplies the early-exit/completion behaviour a transducer's completion step provides. The classic form (a Transducer alias over FnMut(Acc, A) -> Acc) is justified only when the pipeline must be stored as a single type independent of the source (Box<dyn Fn(...)> in a library) or must drive a non-Iterator sink such as a channel send.
code_sketch:
let src = 0u32..;                                  // any IntoIterator
let out: Vec<u32> = src
    .filter(|x| x % 2 == 0)
    .map(|x| x * x)
    .take(3)                                       // lazy: adapters do nothing yet
    .collect();                                    // terminal chooses the sink
let sum: u32 = (0..1_000_000).filter(|x| x % 2 == 0).map(|x| x * x).sum();
// stateful stage: .scan(0u32, |st, x| { *st += x; Some(*st) })
pitfalls: Adapters are lazy and #[must_use]: a chain that is never consumed compiles (with a warning) and does nothing at all.
An iterator is single-use: re-iterating needs a fresh source, a clone or by_ref, and storing a chain in a struct needs a lifetime or move closures over owned data.
Boxing the pipeline into Box<dyn Iterator<Item = T>> is the only way to store it as one named type and adds dynamic dispatch per element; prefer impl Iterator or collect.
Iterator::scan state lives in the iterator, so cloning or re-using the iterator duplicates or resets the running state.
